entry.title: Rewriting Git History with Interactive Rebase
entry.summary:
Hello friends, In this third article of our Git in Depth series, we'll try to learn and understand the topic of "interactive rebase". As you can tell from the title, interactive rebase is used to change/rewrite our git history. However, we need to keep the following warning in mind. Never rebase shared commits. Changes made to the past, especially on remote repos, can be very exhausting. But again, for example, if a piece of information that shouldn't have been shared was written to the history, it may need to be deleted. For this, the best method is actually to delete a specific file or text from the entire history with the BFG tool. For details, you can check out this link. entry.title: Git in Depth 1: How Git Works
entry.summary:
Hello, in this article we'll try to examine how Git organizes and manages files. Basically, Git performs four fundamental functions. Distribution of Repositories (Distributed Structure) Branching and Corrections Versioning and Content Tracking Storing objects as key-value pairs.
Let's start examining from the inside out. Key Value Store The hash (sha1) of every file is kept, and changes are tracked on top of it. Folders, and even commits, have a hash too. For example, with the code below we get the hash of a string input. echo "merhaba dünya" | git hash-object --stdin
# 2ad1d25f2216c4cf25cbfb508d485f2350f317d8
If we make even the slightest change to this string, the hash changes. This means the file has changed. echo "merhaba dünya " | git hash-object --stdin dd38a8c3d16d052a1b43ad96172…

entry.summary: Healthcare AI systems depend on accurate patient records. However, integrating information from multiple sources creates an important challenge: establishing that the records being analysed belong to the same individual. A model can process data accurately and still produce an unsafe recommendation if patient identity is incorrect. entry.title: EVA: An Arch-Based Linux Desktop Built Around a Custom Wayland Shell
entry.summary:
EVA is an independent Linux distribution based on Arch Linux. Its goal is to offer a complete, integrated desktop experience built around its own Wayland compositor and desktop shell. It is currently in beta and targets x86_64 systems. It uses the Calamares installer and includes desktop components such as workspace management, notifications, system settings, a dock and panel, bundled applications, and a game center.
Project and source code: https://github.com/2207juan/EVA
ISO downloads: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1uZRp9SGSDykXUKvbprnLntPWDCimsDnt?usp=sharing
EVA is still in beta, so feedback, bug reports, and suggestions are welcome through the project repository. If you try it, I’d especially like to hear how the desktop behaves on your hardware and what would make installation or daily use clearer.
